result: Loss of DLK and/or LZK, singly or in combination, does not cause discernible defects in Purkinje cells. The authors generated an LZK knockout mouse line and crossed it with conditional DLK knockout mice using PvalbCre to delete these kinases in Purkinje cells. Histological analysis, Purkinje cell counts, molecular layer thickness, astrocyte markers, and body weight were all normal in these knockout mice at P60.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed these findings, stating 'Novel findings include that DLK and LZK are dispensable for proper cerebellar Purkinje cell development' in the acceptance summary. The data supporting normal Purkinje cell development in knockout mice (Figure 1) were not questioned by any reviewer.

result: Activating DLK causes rapid death of Purkinje cells through JNK activation and caspase-mediated apoptosis. The authors generated Cre-inducible DLK overexpression transgenic mice (Hipp11-DLK(iOE)) and crossed them with PvalbCre mice. These mice showed gross abnormalities by P6, smaller body size, abnormal movements, death by P21, nearly complete (~98%) Purkinje cell loss, increased astrocyte and microglia reactivity, and elevated p-c-Jun levels.
evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this finding in the acceptance summary: 'increased DLK or LZK activity is sufficient to drive Purkinje cell death.' The data showing rapid DLK-induced degeneration (Figure 2) were accepted without challenge, though reviewers requested clarification about the broader expression pattern of PvalbCre (Essential Revision 1).

result: Activating LZK leads to slow degeneration of Purkinje cells with JNK activation and caspase-mediated apoptosis. PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-LZK(iOE)/+ mice survived to adulthood (up to 8 months) but showed low body weight, morphological abnormalities of Purkinje cells starting around P15, progressive cell loss from P21 to P120, reduced cerebellum and molecular layer area, increased astrocyte reactivity, elevated p-c-Jun, and cleaved caspase-3 in Purkinje cells.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as a major contribution, noting in the acceptance summary that 'increased DLK or LZK activity is sufficient to drive Purkinje cell death.' Reviewer 3 requested clarification about the rostral-caudal expression differences in LZK overexpression (Essential Revision 3), which the authors addressed, but the core finding was not challenged.

result: DLK overexpression induces JNK activation (p-c-Jun), apoptosis (TUNEL, cleaved caspase-3), dendrite swelling, and cytoskeletal disruption (decreased MAP2 and NF-200) in Purkinje cells. The peak of dendrite swelling and apoptosis occurred around P15, with ~65% of swollen dendrites positive for cleaved caspase-3.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these mechanistic findings without challenge. Reviewer 2 requested additional images to illustrate dendrite swelling quantification (Essential Revision 2), indicating engagement with the data rather than skepticism. The data in Figure 3 supporting these claims were not disputed.

result: Deleting CELF2 does not modify phenotypes caused by increased DLK expression. PvalbCre/+;Celf2fl/fl;Hipp11-DLK(iOE)/+ mice showed similar Purkinje cell degeneration, p-c-Jun induction, smaller cerebellum, morbidity, low body weight, and death around P21 as PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-DLK(iOE)/+ mice.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding as part of the differential signaling mechanism between DLK and LZK. The acceptance summary notes the work provides 'data supporting the conclusions drawn regarding the roles of DLK and LZK in the cerebellum,' and this specificity was not questioned.

result: Deleting CELF2 strongly attenuates Purkinje cell degeneration induced by LZK, but not DLK, partly via regulating alternative splicing of Map2k7. PvalbCre/+;Celf2fl/fl;Hipp11-LZK(iOE)/+ mice showed significantly improved behavioral phenotypes, dramatically reduced Purkinje cell degeneration, improved dendrite morphology, reduced astrogliosis and microgliosis, rescued MAP2 and NF-200 levels, attenuated p-c-Jun intensity, and reduced cleaved caspase-3 signals compared to PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-LZK(iOE)/+ mice. CELF2 deletion reduced the Map2k7-S/Map2k7-L mRNA ratio by ~20%.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding in the acceptance summary, stating the work provides 'data supporting the conclusions drawn regarding the roles of DLK and LZK in the cerebellum.' The differential effect of CELF2 deletion on LZK versus DLK signaling (Figures 5-6) was accepted as a key mechanistic distinction and was not challenged.

result: Each kinase (DLK and LZK) induces Purkinje cell degeneration largely independent of each other. Deletion of LZK did not prevent DLK-induced degeneration (PvalbCre/+;Map3k13KO/KO;Hipp11-DLK(iOE)/+ mice showed similar phenotypes to PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-DLK(iOE)/+), and deletion of DLK did not prevent LZK-induced degeneration (PvalbCre/+;Map3k12fl/fl;Hipp11-LZK(iOE)/+ mice resembled PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-LZK(iOE)/+).
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding without challenge. The data in Figure 7 demonstrating independent action of each kinase were not questioned, and this conclusion aligns with the reviewers' acceptance of the differential signaling mechanisms between DLK and LZK.

result: Body weight loss, motor deficits, and early mortality were associated with PvalbCre/+;Hipp11-DLK(iOE)/+ pups, but the authors infer these gross abnormalities are unlikely the consequence of Purkinje cell death alone, given that Parvalbumin-Cre is expressed widely throughout the nervous system.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly raised concerns about interpretation of these systemic phenotypes in Essential Revision 1, stating 'interpretation of phenotypes such as behavior or early mortality is complex' and 'the extreme phenotypes observed for body weight and motor behavior phenotypes are unlikely the consequence of Purkinje cell death alone, and this should be discussed.' The authors acknowledged this limitation but did not provide additional data to clarify the cellular basis of these phenotypes.

result: PvalbCre induces higher levels of transgene expression in anterior cerebellum than posterior, correlating with more severe Purkinje cell pathology and reduced MAP2 levels in the anterior region in LZK overexpression mice.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically asked about rostral versus caudal expression differences (Essential Revision 3), and the authors' data showing this gradient (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E) were accepted. The reviewer's question was about whether this explained the less severe LZK phenotype compared to DLK, which the authors addressed by showing comparable tdTomato mRNA levels from both transgenes.

result: DLK is localized to somas, dendrites, and axons of Purkinje cells and regulates the neuronal cytoskeleton. The dendritic cytoskeleton in Purkinje cells may be prone to disruption upon aberrant DLK activation.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these findings. The data showing DLK localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and cytoskeletal disruption were accepted as consistent with known roles of DLK in regulating microtubule stability, as cited in the manuscript.

result: Deleting LZK does not disrupt Purkinje cell morphology, but increasing LZK expression causes reduced neurofilament levels in the molecular layer, disorganization of the pinceau at the axon initial segment, and decreased MAP2 levels in dendrites. CELF2 deletion restores MAP2 levels in LZK overexpression mice.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as part of the characterization of LZK effects on Purkinje cells. The data in Figures 4-5 supporting these claims were not challenged, and these observations contribute to the mechanistic understanding of LZK-induced degeneration.
